Thank you once again for your thoughtful follow-up and for the constructive suggestions throughout the review process. We greatly appreciate your engagement and are encouraged by your decision to raise the score.

Regarding your comment on the Related Work section, we fully agree that image-to-SVG generation is a crucial counterpart to text-to-SVG, and deserves more in-depth coverage. - SuperSVG [1], which leverages superpixel-based decomposition for semantic-preserving vectorization
- Layered Vectorization [2], which introduces semantic simplification strategies to produce structured, layered SVGs

We will also briefly reflect on how insights from both text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG approaches can complement each other and inspire future multimodal directions.

More broadly, we confirm that the Related Work section will be updated to explicitly cite and discuss all four approaches mentioned during the review and rebuttal phases. In particular, we have already included comparative experiments with OmniSVG and LLM4SVG, following the recent availability of their models, and we will integrate both these results and their corresponding methodological discussions in the final version of the paper.

We are grateful for your guidance and look forward to incorporating these improvements.

I suggest that the authors provide a more comprehensive overview of the related fields, as both text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG are crucial for the development of SVG assets. The authors should consider discussing some recent image-to-SVG methods [1,2], and it would be even better to explore the insights and potential that these two approaches offer for SVG asset construction. In summary, I will raise my score.

[1] Hu T, Yi R, Qian B, et al. Supersvg: Superpixel-based scalable vector graphics synthesis[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2024: 24892-24901.

rebuttal.value:
We are grateful to the reviewer for its thoughtful and constructive comments on our submission. Your suggestions have helped us clarify and strengthen several aspects of our work. Our detailed responses are provided below.

 > ### W1: Quality of machine-generated descriptions

We recognize this as an important concern about dataset quality. To address both this point and related weakness number 3 about human evaluation, we conducted a comprehensive user study measuring both image quality and image-text semantic alignment.
We asked 29 participants to assess images generated by six different methods using captions from our HeisenVec test set, plus ground truth images. Participants were asked to rate two different aspects on a 5-point scale: (i) visual quality of the image independently from the text description, (ii) semantic correlation between the image and its accompanying text description.
After collecting 1,049 total evaluations, the ground truth images achieved an average image-text correlation score of 4.12 out of 5. This high rating demonstrates that our automated captioning process produces descriptions with strong semantic alignment, despite not involving human validation during creation.
The user study results validate our approach: while the descriptions are machine-generated, they maintain sufficient quality and accuracy for training purposes. Human evaluators consistently found the image-text pairs to be well-aligned and meaningful.
To further strengthen our dataset quality claims, we will add quantitative CLIP scores measuring the semantic similarity between each caption and its corresponding image to the HeisenVec train and test sets. Since each image in HeisenVec includes four different textual descriptions, this will provide additional evidence of consistent image-text alignment across multiple description variants. However, we already showed in Table 1 of the main paper that HeisenVec has a higher overall CLIP-Score compared to other datasets. 

> ### W2: Long-context modeling challenges and mitigation strategies

This aspect correctly identifies a fundamental challenge in our task: SVG generation represents an inherently divergent problem where brief text prompts must condition the generation of much longer, structured output sequences. This amplification from input to output creates unique difficulties that differ from typical language modeling scenarios.
We designed HeisenVec specifically to support research into generating complex vector graphics that require extended context understanding. Our current approach focuses on several mitigation strategies to handle long sequences more effectively. We developed specialized preprocessing techniques that reduce the required context window while preserving essential structural information, and we introduced an additional set of domain-specific tokens to create more efficient representations of SVG elements.
However, we acknowledge that our current work represents an initial baseline rather than a complete solution to long-context challenges. The performance degradation we observe with longer sequences reflects the broader difficulty of maintaining coherent generation over extended outputs: a problem that extends beyond our specific domain.
The analysis of these limitations and the development of more sophisticated mitigation strategies represent important directions for future work. We believe HeisenVec provides a solid foundation for this research by offering a large-scale, high-quality, standardized dataset that enables systematic investigation of long-context generation challenges in the text-to-SVG domain.

> ### W3: Human evaluation, error analysis, and failure case studies

**Human Evaluation Results**

With reference to the user study introduced in W1, we now present in the following table the additional results related to human evaluation, showing the average ratings given by users.

Our user study assessed both image quality and text-image alignment across six generation methods:

|    Models    | Image Quality Ranking |

We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to methodological details, especially regarding the choice of generative paradigms for SVG creation. This is an important point, and we address it thoroughly in the responses below.

> ### W1: Comparison with diffusion-based approaches

Regarding diffusion-based methods, we believe there's a fundamental mismatch between these approaches and the text-to-SVG generation task. Diffusion models operate in RGB pixel space and are designed for rasterized image generation, whereas SVGs exist as structured vector representations. This creates several practical issues: diffusion methods cannot directly produce the discrete symbolic commands that define SVG paths, and any diffusion-to-SVG pipeline would require an additional conversion step that introduces potential quality degradation. Moreover, these methods require a larger amount of time compared to autoregressive approaches.
We also considered “LayerDiffuse” [1] as suggested by the reviewer, but we found that it addresses a significantly different problem: generating layered rasterized images with foreground/background separation rather than vector graphics synthesis. In case the reviewer was referring to a different project, we would be more than happy to investigate and include it in the final version of our work.
Also, we would like to point out that we included diffusion-based baselines in our evaluation. VectorFusion and SVGDreamer (shown in the first two rows of Table 2 of the main paper) represent the current state-of-the-art within this approach adapted for vector graphics. We acknowledge these baselines could be presented more prominently and will clarify their appearance in the final version of our paper.
Our central idea is to approach SVG generation as a structured text generation task, remaining entirely within the text domain. This approach not only offers computational efficiency and high representational fidelity, but also avoids the scalability constraints associated with image resolution, which are inherent in methods that rely on rasterized representations.

> ### W2: Float numbers tokenization approach

This is indeed a critical challenge in LLM-based vector graphics generation. Our solution centers on coordinate quantization combined with canvas scaling to avoid floating-point representation entirely.
As detailed in Section 1 of our supplementary materials, we scale up the canvas dimensions and cast all coordinates to integers. This quantization introduces minimal error that remains imperceptible from a human visual perspective while dramatically simplifying the tokenization process. Using the standard Llama3 tokenizer, each coordinate pair is represented by exactly three tokens in the format px<|SEP|>py; where px, py and <|SEP|> are single tokens. This creates a highly regular and predictable token structure.
Due to the limited time available for the rebuttal and considering that reviewer BNfS raised a closely related point, we prioritized what we view as the most impactful ablation. Specifically, we trained a version of our model without applying path command reduction and coordinate quantization in the preprocessing pipeline. Results are reported in the table below:

|   vHector 3B  |   CLIP-S  |   DINO-S  | HPSv2     |
|:-------------:|:---------:|:---------:|-----------|
| **w/out std** |   64.37   |   38.45   | 13.91     |
|   **w/ std**  | **67.83** | **48.52** | **14.84** |

The integer approach delivers substantial improvements across all metrics. Beyond the computational benefits, this quantization strategy reduces the entropy of the coordinate space. The model learns from a more constrained and regular distribution of possible values rather than the virtually infinite space of floating-point numbers. This constraint actually enhances learning by eliminating meaningless precision variations while preserving all visually relevant information.
Our approach thus addresses the tokenization challenge by fundamentally restructuring the representation space rather than trying to efficiently encode problematic floating-point values.

[1] Zhang, Lvmin, and Maneesh Agrawala. "Transparent image layer diffusion using latent transparency." arXiv preprint arXiv:2402.17113 (2024).

> ### W1 & W2 : Comparison with OmniSVG and LLM4SVG frameworks

We acknowledge the importance of benchmarking against these recent methods. At the time of our original submission, the official model weights for both OmniSVG [1] and LLM4SVG [2] were not publicly available, which precluded their inclusion in our comparative analysis. Following the recent release of these weights, we have conducted comprehensive evaluations of both methods on the HeisenVec test set. The results are presented in the table below, demonstrating that vHector maintains superior performance across all evaluation metrics.

| Models   |   CLIP-S  |   DINO-S  |   HPSv2   |
|------------|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|

We also point out that the released data for the OmniSVG dataset seems to be incomplete and its related test set is missing. This prevented us from directly testing vHector on the OmniSVG dataset.

We commit to including these comparative results in the final version of our paper. Additionally, we will gladly extend our evaluation to include the complete OmniSVG dataset and test set once they become available, ensuring a more exhaustive assessment of our method's performance relative to the state-of-the-art.

 > ### W3: Demonstrating HeisenVec's effectiveness through cross-dataset evaluation

To address this concern, we conducted additional experiments training our vHector 3B model on the alternative datasets mentioned by the reviewer, after pre-processing them through our standardization approach. Given the time constraints for this rebuttal, we applied only the first alignment stage from our training pipeline: this means fine-tuning for 6 epochs from the pretrained LLaMa 3.2 3B model.

The results below demonstrate HeisenVec clear advantages over these existing datasets (FT means Fine Tuning).

| Models     |   CLIP-S  |   DINO-S  |   HPSv2   |
|--------------|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|
| **FT_SVGX-Core** |   62.98   |   35.36   |   13.98   |
| **FT_ColorSVG**  |   58.86   |   31.46   |   12.83   |
| **vHector 3B**   | **67.83** | **48.52** | **14.84** |

These experiments provide direct evidence that HeisenVec scale and diversity translate into meaningful performance gains. The consistent improvements across all metrics suggest that our dataset's design choices effectively support better model generalization compared to the abovementioned SVG resources. We will integrate these new results in the final version of our paper.

> ### W4:  Analysis of long-context SVGs and model scaling effects

This is an important observation that touches on a core challenge in text-to-SVG generation. The task becomes particularly demanding when models must generate lengthy, complex SVG sequences from relatively brief text prompts: essentially expanding short inputs into much longer, structured outputs.
We designed the HeisenVec dataset specifically to address complex image generation requiring extended context understanding. While our current work focuses on preprocessing and tokenization strategies to manage long sequences more effectively, we recognize this opens several promising research directions for future exploration.
To directly address model size and context length interactions, we conducted targeted experiments comparing our vHector 3B and vHector 8B models across different context windows (2k and 8k tokens with corresponding test sets), as reported below:

Conversely, the smaller 3B model experiences a performance drop with longer contexts, especially on DINO-S, supporting the hypothesis that larger models are better suited to handle long SVG sequences without degrading performance on shorter sequences.

summary.value: This paper introduces HeisenVec, a large-scale dataset of 2.2 million SVGs paired with multi-source textual descriptions, designed to advance text-to-SVG generation using large language models (LLMs). The dataset undergoes rigorous standardization to convert SVGs into a unified token space, prioritizing structural consistency and long-context modeling (up to 32k tokens). The authors also present vHector, an LLM-based model family (built on LLaMA 3.1/3.2) with custom SVG tokens, enabling direct autoregressive SVG generation. Experiments show vHector outperforms prior LLM-based methods in structural validity and prompt alignment, though it still lags behind diffusion-based approaches. The release includes the dataset, tokenization tools, and evaluation pipelines to foster research in vector graphics generation.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper proposes HeisenVec, a million-scale dataset for text-to-SVG, featuring diverse styles and long sequences (mean length 24k characters), addressing a critical gap in vector graphics research.
2. vHector leverages LLMs’ sequence modeling strengths with domain-specific tokens, enabling direct SVG generation without raster intermediates, which improves structural coherence.
3. The paper provides rigorous evaluation metrics (CLIP-S, FID, HPS v2) and open-source tools, promoting reproducibility and setting a standard for future work.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The dataset and models are not benchmarked against the latest OmniSVG framework [1], which may hinder the evaluation of HeisenVec’s competitiveness in the rapidly evolving field of SVG generation.

2. The paper omits direct performance comparisons with LLM4SVG [2]—a prior LLM-based SVG generation method—despite referencing it in the related work. This absence limits the ability to quantify the advancement of vHector in the context of existing LLM-driven approaches.

3. To validate HeisenVec’s effectiveness, the authors do not train vHector on alternative SVG datasets (e.g., ColorSVG, SVGX-Core) and compare performance. This prevents a direct demonstration of whether the dataset’s scale and diversity truly enable superior model generalization compared to prior resources.

4. The paper does not analyze how the inclusion of large, long-context SVGs influences model performance. Key questions remain unanswered: Do long sequences enhance generative capabilities for complex graphics, or do they degrade basic generation accuracy? Are larger models (e.g., vHector-8B) better suited to handle long SVGs, while smaller models (e.g., vHector-3B) struggle to maintain performance on shorter sequences when trained on long data? This gap hinders understanding of the dataset’s optimal usage and model scaling dynamics.


[1] Yang Y, Cheng W, Chen S, et al. Omnisvg: A unified scalable vector graphics generation model[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.06263, 2025.
[2] Xing X, Hu J, Liang G, et al. Empowering llms to understand and generate complex vector graphics[C]//Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025: 19487-19497.

summary.value: This paper presents HeisenVec, a large-scale dataset comprising 2.2 million standardized SVGs paired with diverse, multi-source textual captions, specifically curated for advancing text-to-vector-graphics generation. To fully exploit this dataset, the authors introduce vHector, a family of autoregressive models built upon the LLaMA 3.1/3.2 architecture. These models are enhanced with long-context LoRA adapters and domain-specific tokens to ensure syntactic validity and geometric coherence in the generated SVG outputs.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Novel Dataset: This is the first million-scale SVG dataset featuring long sequences, addressing a significant gap in vector graphics research. The authors implement a robust standardization pipeline that enforces structural consistency across samples and facilitates efficient autoregressive training. Additionally, the use of a multi-captioning strategy—leveraging BLIP2, Florence2, and Idefics3—substantially improves the semantic alignment between text and SVG content.

- The paper employs a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics to assess both dataset diversity and model performance. Notably, vHector-8B outperforms previous LLM and diffusion-based approaches.

limitations_weaknesses.value: - The paper offers limited ablation studies on the effects of specific standardization decisions (e.g., path command reduction, coordinate quantization), which could impact downstream model performance.

summary.value:
HeisenVec is a new large-scale dataset created for generating vector graphics from natural language. Unlike datasets for raster images, HeisenVec focuses on Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG), which are represented by drawing commands and style attributes. It contains 2.2 million SVGs, each with four textual descriptions generated by multi-modal models.

To ensure consistency for autoregressive modeling, all SVGs are standardized by unifying geometric primitives, applying transformations, and compressing syntax with custom tokens. HeisenVec covers a wide range of visual styles and sequence lengths, with many samples exceeding 8,000 tokens, making it suitable for benchmarking long-context language models.

strengths_contributions.value:
This problem is worth exploring, and indeed lacks a high-quality large scale dataset for this task. The proposed method is valuable and can greatly boost the research in this area.

The dataset enables rigorous evaluation of text-conditioned SVG generation, promotes progress in sequence modeling with symbolic outputs, and connects vision, graphics, and language research. The dataset, tokenization tools, and evaluation pipeline are openly available to support further research.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
I lean to accept this paper, and have two issues to further discuss here
1. Should LLMs be the right way to model this problem? Some diffusion-based methods such as LayerDiffusion can also address the layered generation task in a good way. Besides, should some diffusion-based baselines be included in the comparisons? I only see some LLMs results in the current version.
2. How do you resolve the tokenization of float numbers? This is a common issue in CAD and SVG generation when being used on LLMs.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: This paper proposed a solid method and the rebuttal has addressed all my concerns. I still lean to accept this paper for the DB track.

summary.value: This paper presents HeisenVec, a large-scale dataset of over 2.2 million standardized SVGs paired with multi-captioned textual descriptions, enabling structured, long-context text-to-vector generation. The authors introduce vHector, a family of LLM-based models fine-tuned on this dataset, using a hybrid tokenizer with SVG-specific tokens. They demonstrate that vHector models outperform previous baselines in both structural validity and semantic alignment, especially for long SVG sequences (up to 32k tokens).

strengths_contributions.value:
1.Novel Dataset Contribution: HeisenVec is the most comprehensive and large-scale text-to-SVG dataset to date, with long sequence lengths and multi-source captioning.
2.New Benchmark Task: The paper clearly formalizes the task of text-to-SVG as autoregressive sequence generation in a symbolic domain.
3.Model Design: The vHector models extend LLaMA with a compact set of 17 SVG-domain tokens, improving syntactic correctness and alignment.
4.Strong Empirical Results:vHector outperforms LLM-based and diffusion-based baselines across all reported metrics (CLIP-S, FID, HPSv2, SSIM, LPIPS, DINO-S).
5.Reproducibility & Open Science: Dataset, tokenizer, models, and evaluation scripts are planned for release, encouraging broad adoption.
6.Scalable Design: Long-context generation is explored with up to 32k tokens, showing practical scalability of LLMs in structured domains.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.All image descriptions are machine-generated, without human validation. There is no quantitative check on text-image semantic alignment quality.
2.Long-Context Modeling Challenges Unexplained: Performance drops notably for longer sequences, but no analysis or mitigation strategies are provided.
3.The paper lacks detailed human evaluation, error typology, or case studies of model failure.
4.Foundation vision-language models like GPT-4V or Claude 3 are not compared, though they could be adapted to this task.
5.No Statistical Significance Reporting: Results are reported as point estimates only, without error bars or variance analysis.

title.value: vHector and HeisenVec: Scalable Vector Graphics Generation Through Large Language Models

TLDR.value: Generation of images in SVG format through LLMs without exploiting their rasterized version

abstract.value: We introduce HeisenVec, a large-scale dataset designed to advance research in vector graphics generation from natural language descriptions. Unlike conventional image generation datasets that focus on raster images, HeisenVec targets the structured and symbolic domain of Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG), where images are represented as sequences of drawing commands and style attributes. The dataset comprises 2.2 million SVGs collected from different online sources, each paired with four complementary textual descriptions generated by multi-modal models. To ensure structural consistency and efficiency for autoregressive modeling, all SVGs are standardized through a pre-processing pipeline that unifies geometric primitives as paths, applies affine transformations, and compresses syntax via custom tokens set. HeisenVec exhibits broad coverage among visual styles and sequence lengths, with a substantial portion of samples exceeding 8,000 tokens, making it particularly well-suited for benchmarking long-context language models. Our benchmark enables rigorous evaluation of text-conditioned SVG generation, encourages progress on sequence modeling with symbolic outputs, and bridges the gap between vision, graphics, and language. We release the dataset, tokenization tools, and evaluation pipeline to foster further research in this emerging domain.
